newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly won't end rent controls for vacancies.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly won't end rent controls for vacancies.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker on Tuesday signalled how little room there was to reach a compromise over the crucial issue of apartment rent rules, saying ending them for vacancies was a poor idea.

"All I say is that there is an old saying, those who fail to study history are doomed to repeat it. I suggest that all of the sentators look at the 1971 to 1974 experiment on vacancy decontrol and come up with a better way," Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, told reporters in Albany.

Under former Republican Gov Nelson Rockefeller, apartments that became vacant during that period were de-controlled, which spurred some unscrupulous landlords to try to push tenants out, by not providing them with hot water, for example, according to a spokeswoman for Assemblyman Vito Lopez, D-King's County, who chairs the body's housing committee.
"So after that was done, it was quickly put back bacause there was such harrassment of tenants," she said.

Gov George Pataki, who wants to negotiate a compromise over the issue, which mainly affects New York City as it has nearly one million rent-regulated apartments, has said he favored letting landlords charge market rents for apartments that become vacant.
This is a milder position than the one pushed by Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, who wants to end the rules in two years, except for the needy, disabled and elderly.
The present apartment rental regulations expire on June 15, and little action is expected on a new budget for fiscal 1998, which was due on April 1, until this battle is solved.
Asked whether he would agree some changes in rent rules, Silver said: "I am prepared to allow public debate to dictate the final conclusion of the issue."

While New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani saw progress in his talks on rent rules with Albany lawmakers on Monday, Silver said he did not give the mayor any reason for that judgment. Giuliani had mentioned providing more state aid for building new housing as part of a possible compromise, and Silver noted that the Assembly last week proposed spending $193 million more to make housing more affordable and pay for structural repairs.

Silver again pressed the Senate to approve its own measure on rent regulations, a step that would allow the issue to be taken up by a conference committee between the two house. The Assembly already has approved its own legislation, which would extend the rent rules.

The Speaker said that if the conference included a handful of Republican senators from New York City and nearby areas that also are affected, rent rules likely would be made permanent, as the issue would be important enough for them to oppose the Senate Majority Leader.
